screens.title: Read and Write Paths: Understanding Data Flow
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we'll follow how Cassandra handles data from the moment a client issues a write or read until the system confirms durability or returns a result. You'll learn why the commit log guarantees durability, how memtables act as an in-memory buffer, and how immutable SSTables on disk become the durable representation of your data. We'll also trace the read path: how a coordinator locates replicas, how caches and Bloom filters reduce disk access, and how reconciliation and read repair keep replicas consistent. Practical examples will show you how to observe commit log and SSTable files and how flush and compaction shape on-disk data. This understanding matters because many production performance and safety decisions come from these internals: where to place the commit log, when write latency matters, and why poorly designed queries can be slow even on a healthy cluster. By the end of this lesson you'll be able to explain the lifecycle of a write, identify read-time optimizations, and spot common misconfigurations that threaten durability or increase latency. Consider how you might check a slow write or a surprising read result in your own deployment as we explore the details.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to trace the full lifecycle of a write from client to durable disk files and explain why the commit log is critical for durability. You will understand the role of the memtable as an in-memory buffer and how, when flushed, it becomes SSTables that store immutable sorted key-value entries. You will describe the read path, including how a coordinator locates replicas, consults caches and Bloom filters, and reads SSTables to reconstruct the most recent row. Finally, you will identify common operational mistakes such as disabling durable writes or placing the commit log on slow storage, and understand preventive practices. Each objective ties to practical checks you can perform: looking at commit log files, forcing a memtable flush to observe SSTables, and interpreting read latencies to detect ineffective Bloom filters or excessive SSTables. These skills matter because internal behavior directly affects performance, durability, and consistency. Knowing what to inspect will let you troubleshoot slow reads, missing data after a crash, or uneven replica states with confidence.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Applied Skills
screens.narratorSegment: These applied objectives translate conceptual understanding into action. You will learn how to inspect commit log files on disk and how to force a memtable flush so you can see SSTable creation. You'll practice interpreting the file names and extensions you find in the data directory to distinguish SSTable components from commit logs. screens.title: Write Path Overview
screens.narratorSegment: When a client issues a write, the cluster first assigns a coordinator node for that request. The coordinator enforces the requested consistency level and begins two local actions before confirming durability. First, it appends the mutation to the commit log, an append-only file that guarantees the write can be recovered if the node crashes. Second, it writes the same data to the memtable, an in-memory, sorted buffer that accumulates writes. After these local steps, the coordinator forwards the mutation to each replica responsible for the partition key. Each replica repeats the commit log append and memtable update. The coordinator awaits acknowledgements from enough replicas as required by the consistency level and then responds to the client. If a replica is down, hinted handoff allows the coordinator to store a short-lived hint to replay the missed mutation when the replica returns. This sequence matters because the commit log provides crash recovery while the memtable provides fast in-memory access that later becomes SSTables when flushed. A common misconception is that memtables alone provide durability; they don't—without the commit log a crash can lose data. Another pitfall is assuming the coordinator stores the only durable copy; in a replicated setup, every replica must persist the mutation. Consider this flow the backbone of Cassandra's write durability and availability model.

1

Diagram: logical flow
Client
Coordinator
Replica nodes
Client

screens.title: Commit Log: The Durability Backbone
screens.narratorSegment: The commit log is Cassandra's primary durability mechanism. Every write is appended to the commit log before the system acknowledges it to the client. This append-only design ensures that, if a node crashes before its memtables are flushed to SSTables, the mutation can be replayed from the commit log during startup to reconstruct lost in-memory state. Think of the commit log as a sequential journal of recent mutations that serves crash recovery and ordering. A practical example is when you temporarily observe a node crash right after many writes: without the commit log, those recent writes would vanish; with it, the node replays the log and recovers the memtable. Common mistakes include disabling durable writes for convenience or placing the commit log on slow or unreliable storage. If durable_writes is false, data that has only been written to memtable may be lost on crash. If the commit log resides on slow disks, write latency suffers because Cassandra waits for the append to complete before acknowledging the client. A good safe practice is to place the commit log on fast, reliable storage separate from SSTable directories. Remember: memtables provide speed, but commit logs provide safety. Ask yourself how you would verify the commit log in a running instance if your application reported lost recent writes.

keyIdea.title: Commit log role
keyIdea.text: An append-only, per-node transaction log that enables crash recovery; misconfiguring it risks data loss or high write latency.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Commit Log
Definition
An append-only transaction log where each write is recorded before acknowledgement, enabling replay after crashes.
Concrete example
If a node crashes immediately after receiving a write, the commit log entry allows reconstruction of the memtable on restart so no acknowledged write is lost.
Why it matters
  • Provides crash recovery for recent writes.
  • Blocks write acknowledgement until the append completes, so disk speed affects write latency.
  • Poor placement or disabling durable writes introduces risk of data loss.
Operational notes
Inspect commit log directory to see files like CommitLog-6-123456789.log. Keep commit log on fast, reliable storage separated from the data directory.
Common mistakes
Turning off durable_writes or putting the commit log on a slow disk. Both reduce resilience or increase latency.
Key Takeaway

Commit log write is the necessary durable step for every acknowledged write; treat it as primary safety-critical storage.

screens.title: Memtable, Flush, and SSTable Timeline
screens.narratorSegment: Memtables are the in-memory, sorted buffers that accept new writes after the commit log append. They provide fast in-memory reads for recent updates. Over time, as memtables grow or after a configured interval, Cassandra flushes memtables to disk. A flush produces an immutable SSTable containing sorted key-value pairs and auxiliary index and summary files. SSTables are optimized for reads and writes but are never modified in place; updates and deletes create new entries in newer SSTables while earlier files remain unchanged. As more SSTables accumulate, reads may need to merge results from multiple files to produce the latest state of a row. To reclaim space and consolidate updates, the compaction process periodically merges several SSTables into fewer, larger files and drops deleted data marked by tombstones when safe. A common misconception is to expect in-place updates; instead, Cassandra uses append-and-merge semantics. Practically, you can force a memtable flush to see new SSTable files appear in the data directory. Understanding this timeline helps explain why write amplification and read amplification occur and why compaction tuning directly affects both disk usage and read performance.

keyIdea.title: Flush timeline
keyIdea.text: Memtables are flushed to SSTables; SSTables are immutable and later merged by compaction to reduce read overhead and reclaim deleted data.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Memtable & SSTable Timeline
Timeline
Write arrives and commit log is appended
Durable append ensures the mutation is recoverable.
Memtable stores the update in memory
Fast reads of recent writes come from the memtable.
Memtable flush creates SSTable
An immutable on-disk file with sorted data and auxiliary indices.
Compaction merges SSTables
Removes tombstones where safe and reduces read amplification.
Example: force a flush
nodetool flush my_data sensor_readings
This forces the memtable for the table to be written to a new SSTable on disk. After the command, check the data directory to see new .db files.
Key Takeaway

Memtable flushes produce immutable SSTables; compaction later reduces file count and reclaims space.

screens.title: SSTables and Compaction
screens.narratorSegment: SSTables are immutable disk files created when memtables are flushed. Because they are immutable, updates and deletes do not overwrite existing data; instead, newer SSTables contain the latest mutations while older files remain. When a read occurs, Cassandra may need to consult multiple SSTables and the memtable to reconstruct the most recent version of a row. Over time, this leads to many SSTables and potential read amplification. Compaction is the background process that merges several SSTables into fewer, larger files. During compaction Cassandra reconciles versions, drops data that has been deleted and is past its tombstone grace period, and produces consolidated SSTables with fewer overlapping keys. A practical effect is that well-tuned compaction reduces the number of files read for a request, lowering latency. However, compaction also consumes input and output and C P U, so tuning compaction strategy and throughput is an operational trade-off. A common misconception is that compaction immediately deletes old data; in reality, tombstones remain until safe to remove—this avoids resurrecting deleted data on replicas that are temporarily down. Keep in mind that compaction policies and frequency influence read and write amplification, disk usage, and repair behavior.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › SSTables & Compaction
SSTable properties
  • Immutable on-disk files created by memtable flushes.
  • Contain sorted key-value pairs and auxiliary index/summary/filter files.
  • Multiple SSTables can contain different versions of the same partition key.
Why immutability matters
Immutability simplifies concurrent writes and avoids in-place updates, but requires compaction to merge state.
Compaction overview
Compaction selects SSTables and merges them into a smaller set, keeping the latest values and dropping expired tombstones when safe.
Operator note
Compaction reduces read amplification but consumes I/O. Choose a strategy that matches your write and read patterns.
Key Takeaway

Compaction reconciles multiple immutable SSTables to present a single current view of data while reclaiming space from deletions.

Analogy
Think of SSTables as snapshots. Compaction is like consolidating many incremental snapshots into a single clean backup that contains the latest state and removes deleted files.

screens.title: Coordinator Node, Replicas and Hinted Handoff
screens.narratorSegment: The coordinator node is the entry point for client requests in Cassandra; it accepts the request and orchestrates work across replicas. Using the partition key, the coordinator identifies which nodes hold copies of the data and forwards the mutation or read to them. For writes, the coordinator ensures the consistency level is met by waiting for acknowledgements from the configured number of replicas before responding to the client. If a target replica is down, the coordinator can use hinted handoff: it stores a hint locally recording the missed mutation for the unavailable replica. When the replica returns, the coordinator or another node will deliver the hint to bring it up to date. Hinted handoff is an availability mechanism that supports eventual consistency without blocking writes to the rest of the cluster. A common misconception is that hinted handoff replaces repair; it does not. Hinted handoff only holds hints for a short period and is intended for brief outages. For longer periods or wide inconsistencies, full repair or anti-entropy processes are required. In practice, understanding the coordinator's role and hinted handoff behavior helps you reason about write latency, availability during node outages, and when to schedule repairs to maintain long-term consistency.

keyIdea.title: Coordinator role
keyIdea.text: The coordinator orchestrates reads and writes, enforces consistency level, and uses hinted handoff to temporarily store missed writes for down replicas.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Coordinator & Hinted Handoff
Coordinator responsibilities
  • Determine replicas for a partition key.
  • Forward reads and writes to replicas and collect responses.
  • Enforce the configured consistency level before client acknowledgement.
Practical effect
The choice of coordinator affects where client connections go and how latency accumulates across the path to replicas.
Hinted Handoff
If a replica is unavailable, the coordinator stores a small hint recording the missed write. When the replica returns, the hint is delivered so the replica receives the missed mutation.
When it helps
Good for short outages to maintain write availability without requiring manual repair.
Misconception

Hinted handoff is not a replacement for repair. Hints are temporary and not intended for long-term consistency across wide outages.

screens.title: Read Path: From Query to Result
screens.narratorSegment: A read request begins at a coordinator which determines the replica set for the requested partition key. The coordinator sends read requests to enough replicas as required by the consistency level. Each queried replica checks several potential data sources. First it inspects the memtable for the most recent writes that may not yet have been flushed. It may also consult the optional row cache if configured. Next, the replica may consult the partition key cache to find SSTable locations quickly. Before reading SSTables from disk, Cassandra consults each SSTable's Bloom filter to determine if the partition key could be present. If a Bloom filter indicates 'no', the SSTable is skipped, saving disk input and output. If the Bloom filter says 'maybe', Cassandra reads the SSTable to locate keys and return any matching rows. The coordinator receives results from replicas and reconciles differences to produce the most up-to-date row, based on timestamps and tombstones. If inconsistencies are found, the coordinator may initiate read repair in the background to reconcile stale replicas. A typical misconception is that the coordinator always reads all replicas; in practice it queries only the number required by the consistency level, and read repair can be opportunistic. Understanding this flow helps diagnose slow reads and informs when caching or Bloom filter tuning will yield benefits.

keyIdea.title: Read path claim
keyIdea.text: Reads consult memtables, caches, and Bloom filters to limit expensive SSTable disk reads; the coordinator reconciles and may trigger read repair.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Read Path
Read steps
  1. Coordinator determines replica set and issues queries.
  2. Replica checks memtable for recent writes.
  3. Replica consults row cache and partition key cache if enabled.
  4. Bloom filters quickly test whether SSTables might contain the key.
  5. Relevant SSTables are read and results are returned to coordinator.
Key Takeaway

Bloom filters and caches reduce disk I/O; the coordinator reconciles results and enforces consistency requirements.

Example scenario
A client requests a partition key. If the memtable contains the latest write, the replica may return quickly without disk reads. If not, Bloom filters can skip many SSTables; if they indicate a possible hit, only those SSTables are read.
Common mistake
Issuing queries that require full table scans or using ALLOW FILTERING forces heavy SSTable reads and bypasses efficient partition-key-based access patterns.

screens.title: Memtable vs Row Cache vs Partition Key Cache
screens.narratorSegment: Cassandra offers several layers that can reduce read latency: memtable, row cache and partition key cache. The memtable is not a cache in the usual sense; it is the in-memory write buffer that contains the most recent mutations and serves very recent reads. The row cache, when enabled, stores entire rows and can drastically speed up repeated reads for those rows, but it is memory intensive and most effective when read hotspots are stable. In contrast, the partition key cache stores locations of partition keys within SSTables, reducing the amount of index and TOC work needed to find a partition on disk; it is much smaller and cheaper than a full row cache. Choosing which cache to enable depends on workload: a stable set of hot rows can benefit from row cache, while workloads that access many different partitions benefit more from partition key cache and Bloom filters. A common misconception is to enable row cache by default; this often wastes memory for write-heavy or broad-scan workloads. Instead, measure hit rates and memory trade-offs. Understanding these distinctions helps pick the most cost-effective caching strategy to lower read latency without sacrificing memory needed for memtables or system operations.

Understanding these distinctions helps pick the most cost-effective caching strategy to lower read latency without sacrificing memory needed for memtables or system operations.

keyIdea.title: Cache selection
keyIdea.text: Memtable serves fresh writes, row cache stores entire hot rows, partition key cache stores index locations—choose based on access patterns and memory trade-offs.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Cache Comparison
Memtable
In-memory, sorted buffer for recent writes. Provides fast access to the latest state before a flush.
Not optional for writes; part of the write path.
Row Cache (optional)
Stores full rows to speed repeated reads of the same rows. Memory heavy and best for stable hotspots.
Enable only when predictable hot rows exist.
Partition Key Cache
Caches SSTable index locations for partition keys to reduce index lookups on disk. Lightweight and efficient for many read patterns.
Useful when many partitions are accessed but full row caching is impractical.
Decision guide
If a small set of rows are frequently read, consider row cache. For broad partition access patterns, prefer partition key cache and Bloom filter tuning. Always weigh memory cost against latency gains.

screens.title: Bloom Filters: Probabilistic Pre-checks
screens.narratorSegment: A Bloom filter is a compact, probabilistic data structure associated with each SSTable that answers the question: 'Does this SSTable possibly contain this partition key?' It can say either 'definitely not' or 'maybe'. If the Bloom filter returns 'definitely not', Cassandra skips reading that SSTable, saving disk input and output. If it returns 'maybe', Cassandra performs a disk lookup. Bloom filters are space-efficient and tuned with a false positive rate that trades memory for fewer unnecessary reads. A practical consequence is that reads for non-existent keys will be fast when Bloom filters are effective because most SSTables are skipped. However, Bloom filters can produce false positives, leading to occasional unnecessary reads. Common problems include a high false-positive configuration or too many small SSTables (insufficient compaction), both of which increase unnecessary reads. Another issue is corrupted or missing Bloom filter files, which could force disk reads. When diagnosing slow reads for non-existent keys, check Bloom filter false-positive rates and SSTable counts; improving compaction or adjusting filter parameters may reduce latency. Remember that Bloom filters reduce but do not eliminate disk access when keys might exist.

keyIdea.text: A lightweight probabilistic test that avoids many SSTable reads by quickly ruling out files that cannot contain a key, with a configurable false-positive trade-off.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Bloom Filters
What it does
A per-SSTable probabilistic test returning 'definitely not' or 'maybe' for membership of a partition key, enabling SSTable skipping.
Concrete example
A read for a non-existent key consults Bloom filters and skips most SSTables, avoiding costly disk reads when filters are effective.
Limits and checks
  • False positives cause occasional extra disk reads.
  • High SSTable count increases the number of Bloom checks and potential false-positive cost.
  • Check filter settings and compaction if non-existent-key reads are slow.
Common Mistake

Assuming Bloom filters eliminate all disk reads. They reduce work but have a small false positive rate that must be managed.

screens.title: Reconciliation and Read Repair
screens.narratorSegment: When multiple replicas return data for a read, the coordinator reconciles those responses to produce the most up-to-date version of the row. Reconciliation chooses values based on timestamps and honors tombstones for deletions. If the coordinator detects inconsistencies—such as a replica that returns an older value or misses a recent update—it can trigger read repair. Read repair operates as a background write that updates stale replicas with the most recent values discovered during the read. This mechanism provides eventual consistency maintenance without requiring synchronous writes to every replica on every read. A concrete example: if two replicas contain value 'A' and one contains older value 'B', the coordinator will return 'A' to the client and, if read repair is enabled, will asynchronously write 'A' to the stale replica to bring it up to date. A common misconception is that read repair always fixes all inconsistencies instantly; in reality, it is opportunistic and depends on reads hitting inconsistent replicas. For severe or long-standing divergence you should schedule full repair operations. Understanding reconciliation and read repair helps you reason about temporary stale reads and how background processes contribute to cluster consistency over time.

keyIdea.text: Coordinator collects replica responses, reconciles by timestamp and tombstones, and may initiate read repair to update stale replicas asynchronously.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Reconciliation & Read Repair
Reconciliation
Coordinator merges returned results from replicas, selecting newest values by timestamp and respecting tombstones for deletions.
Concrete example
If replicas disagree, the coordinator returns the most recent column values and notes which replicas need updates.
Read repair
An asynchronous write that updates stale replicas discovered during reads. It is opportunistic and relies on reads to detect inconsistencies.
Key Takeaway

Read repair helps maintain eventual consistency by fixing replicas discovered to be stale during normal read traffic.

When to run repair
For prolonged outages or large divergence, schedule full repair/anti-entropy operations; rely on read repair for opportunistic fixes during normal traffic.

screens.title: Observe Commit Log and SSTables — Lab Walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on walkthrough shows the exact commands you can run to observe the write path at the file level. First start a fresh Cassandra instance using Docker and wait for it to initialize. Then connect to cqlsh to create a keyspace and table. Insert a few sample rows so you have recent write activity recorded. Exit cqlsh and list the commit log directory inside the container to see commit log files; these are the raw mutations appended by the write path. Next, force a memtable flush using nodetool flush so Cassandra writes an SSTable to disk. Finally, list the data directory for your keyspace and table to observe SSTable files and supporting files like. db,. filter,. index and. summary. Seeing these files will make the conceptual flow concrete: commit logs separate from the data directory, memtable contents appearing as SSTables when flushed, and multiple supporting files per SSTable. A practical tip: monitor commit log disk usage to avoid filling the partition, and place the commit log on fast storage for consistent write latency. This lab reinforces how the earlier abstract steps appear in a live system.

keyIdea.title: Lab takeaway
keyIdea.text: Running these commands reveals commit log files and SSTable files, making the write-to-disk lifecycle observable and verifiable.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Hands-on Activity
Starter commands (run in a terminal)
docker run --name cassandra-paths -p 9042:9042 -d cassandra:4.1

# connect to cqlsh inside the container
docker exec -it cassandra-paths cqlsh

# create keyspace and table inside cqlsh
CREATE KEYSPACE my_data WITH replication = {'class': 'SimpleStrategy', 'replication_factor': 1};
USE my_data;
CREATE TABLE sensor_readings (
  sensor_id text,
  timestamp timestamp,
  temperature float,
  PRIMARY KEY (sensor_id, timestamp)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (timestamp DESC);
Insert a few rows in cqlsh, then exit to perform filesystem checks.
Inspect files and force flush
# list commit log files
docker exec -it cassandra-paths ls /var/lib/cassandra/commitlog

# force memtable flush to create SSTables
docker exec -it cassandra-paths nodetool flush my_data sensor_readings

# list SSTable files for the table
docker exec -it cassandra-paths ls -l /var/lib/cassandra/data/my_data/sensor_readings-*
Look for CommitLog-*.log files and .db, .filter, .index, .summary files inside the table directory to correlate flush activity with new SSTables.
Reflection
Observe how the commit log files are separate from the data directory. The flush command moves in-memory data to SSTables so you can inspect on-disk representation directly. Use this to verify where writes are stored and to check disk usage patterns.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we'll follow how Cassandra handles data from the moment a client issues a write or read until the system confirms durability or returns a result. You'll learn why the commit log guarantees durability, how memtables act as an in-memory buffer, and how immutable SSTables on disk become the durable representation of your data. We'll also trace the read path: how a coordinator locates replicas, how caches and Bloom filters reduce disk access, and how reconciliation and read repair keep replicas consistent. Practical examples will show you how to observe commit log and SSTable files and how flush and compaction shape on-disk data. This understanding matters because many production performance and safety decisions come from these internals: where to place the commit log, when write latency matters, and why poorly designed queries can be slow even on a healthy cluster. By the end of this lesson you'll be able to explain the lifecycle of a write, identify read-time optimizations, and spot common misconfigurations that threaten durability or increase latency. Consider how you might check a slow write or a surprising read result in your own deployment as we explore the details.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to trace the full lifecycle of a write from client to durable disk files and explain why the commit log is critical for durability. You will understand the role of the memtable as an in-memory buffer and how, when flushed, it becomes SSTables that store immutable sorted key-value entries. You will describe the read path, including how a coordinator locates replicas, consults caches and Bloom filters, and reads SSTables to reconstruct the most recent row. Finally, you will identify common operational mistakes such as disabling durable writes or placing the commit log on slow storage, and understand preventive practices. Each objective ties to practical checks you can perform: looking at commit log files, forcing a memtable flush to observe SSTables, and interpreting read latencies to detect ineffective Bloom filters or excessive SSTables. These skills matter because internal behavior directly affects performance, durability, and consistency. Knowing what to inspect will let you troubleshoot slow reads, missing data after a crash, or uneven replica states with confidence.

These applied objectives translate conceptual understanding into action. You will learn how to inspect commit log files on disk and how to force a memtable flush so you can see SSTable creation. You'll practice interpreting the file names and extensions you find in the data directory to distinguish SSTable components from commit logs. On the read side, you will learn how to reason about Bloom filter effectiveness and partition key cache impacts, and how read repair works to heal inconsistent replicas over time. These tasks matter because they let you validate cluster health and diagnose where to tune configuration or storage placement. For example, you will know when to suspect slow commit log storage if writes are consistently delayed, and when to suspect poor Bloom filter tuning if read queries for non-existent keys scan many SSTables. This objective set closes the loop: theory, observation, and corrective action that improves durability and performance in real deployments.

When a client issues a write, the cluster first assigns a coordinator node for that request. The coordinator enforces the requested consistency level and begins two local actions before confirming durability. First, it appends the mutation to the commit log, an append-only file that guarantees the write can be recovered if the node crashes. Second, it writes the same data to the memtable, an in-memory, sorted buffer that accumulates writes. After these local steps, the coordinator forwards the mutation to each replica responsible for the partition key. Each replica repeats the commit log append and memtable update. The coordinator awaits acknowledgements from enough replicas as required by the consistency level and then responds to the client. If a replica is down, hinted handoff allows the coordinator to store a short-lived hint to replay the missed mutation when the replica returns. This sequence matters because the commit log provides crash recovery while the memtable provides fast in-memory access that later becomes SSTables when flushed. A common misconception is that memtables alone provide durability; they don't—without the commit log a crash can lose data. Another pitfall is assuming the coordinator stores the only durable copy; in a replicated setup, every replica must persist the mutation. Consider this flow the backbone of Cassandra's write durability and availability model.

The commit log is Cassandra's primary durability mechanism. Every write is appended to the commit log before the system acknowledges it to the client. This append-only design ensures that, if a node crashes before its memtables are flushed to SSTables, the mutation can be replayed from the commit log during startup to reconstruct lost in-memory state. Think of the commit log as a sequential journal of recent mutations that serves crash recovery and ordering. A practical example is when you temporarily observe a node crash right after many writes: without the commit log, those recent writes would vanish; with it, the node replays the log and recovers the memtable. Common mistakes include disabling durable writes for convenience or placing the commit log on slow or unreliable storage. If durable_writes is false, data that has only been written to memtable may be lost on crash. If the commit log resides on slow disks, write latency suffers because Cassandra waits for the append to complete before acknowledging the client. A good safe practice is to place the commit log on fast, reliable storage separate from SSTable directories. Remember: memtables provide speed, but commit logs provide safety. Ask yourself how you would verify the commit log in a running instance if your application reported lost recent writes.

Memtables are the in-memory, sorted buffers that accept new writes after the commit log append. They provide fast in-memory reads for recent updates. Over time, as memtables grow or after a configured interval, Cassandra flushes memtables to disk. A flush produces an immutable SSTable containing sorted key-value pairs and auxiliary index and summary files. SSTables are optimized for reads and writes but are never modified in place; updates and deletes create new entries in newer SSTables while earlier files remain unchanged. As more SSTables accumulate, reads may need to merge results from multiple files to produce the latest state of a row. To reclaim space and consolidate updates, the compaction process periodically merges several SSTables into fewer, larger files and drops deleted data marked by tombstones when safe. A common misconception is to expect in-place updates; instead, Cassandra uses append-and-merge semantics. Practically, you can force a memtable flush to see new SSTable files appear in the data directory. Understanding this timeline helps explain why write amplification and read amplification occur and why compaction tuning directly affects both disk usage and read performance.

SSTables are immutable disk files created when memtables are flushed. Because they are immutable, updates and deletes do not overwrite existing data; instead, newer SSTables contain the latest mutations while older files remain. When a read occurs, Cassandra may need to consult multiple SSTables and the memtable to reconstruct the most recent version of a row. Over time, this leads to many SSTables and potential read amplification. Compaction is the background process that merges several SSTables into fewer, larger files. During compaction Cassandra reconciles versions, drops data that has been deleted and is past its tombstone grace period, and produces consolidated SSTables with fewer overlapping keys. A practical effect is that well-tuned compaction reduces the number of files read for a request, lowering latency. However, compaction also consumes input and output and C P U, so tuning compaction strategy and throughput is an operational trade-off. A common misconception is that compaction immediately deletes old data; in reality, tombstones remain until safe to remove—this avoids resurrecting deleted data on replicas that are temporarily down. Keep in mind that compaction policies and frequency influence read and write amplification, disk usage, and repair behavior.

The coordinator node is the entry point for client requests in Cassandra; it accepts the request and orchestrates work across replicas. Using the partition key, the coordinator identifies which nodes hold copies of the data and forwards the mutation or read to them. For writes, the coordinator ensures the consistency level is met by waiting for acknowledgements from the configured number of replicas before responding to the client. If a target replica is down, the coordinator can use hinted handoff: it stores a hint locally recording the missed mutation for the unavailable replica. When the replica returns, the coordinator or another node will deliver the hint to bring it up to date. Hinted handoff is an availability mechanism that supports eventual consistency without blocking writes to the rest of the cluster. A common misconception is that hinted handoff replaces repair; it does not. Hinted handoff only holds hints for a short period and is intended for brief outages. For longer periods or wide inconsistencies, full repair or anti-entropy processes are required. In practice, understanding the coordinator's role and hinted handoff behavior helps you reason about write latency, availability during node outages, and when to schedule repairs to maintain long-term consistency.

A read request begins at a coordinator which determines the replica set for the requested partition key. The coordinator sends read requests to enough replicas as required by the consistency level. Each queried replica checks several potential data sources. First it inspects the memtable for the most recent writes that may not yet have been flushed. It may also consult the optional row cache if configured. Next, the replica may consult the partition key cache to find SSTable locations quickly. Before reading SSTables from disk, Cassandra consults each SSTable's Bloom filter to determine if the partition key could be present. If a Bloom filter indicates 'no', the SSTable is skipped, saving disk input and output. If the Bloom filter says 'maybe', Cassandra reads the SSTable to locate keys and return any matching rows. The coordinator receives results from replicas and reconciles differences to produce the most up-to-date row, based on timestamps and tombstones. If inconsistencies are found, the coordinator may initiate read repair in the background to reconcile stale replicas. A typical misconception is that the coordinator always reads all replicas; in practice it queries only the number required by the consistency level, and read repair can be opportunistic. Understanding this flow helps diagnose slow reads and informs when caching or Bloom filter tuning will yield benefits.

Cassandra offers several layers that can reduce read latency: memtable, row cache and partition key cache. The memtable is not a cache in the usual sense; it is the in-memory write buffer that contains the most recent mutations and serves very recent reads. The row cache, when enabled, stores entire rows and can drastically speed up repeated reads for those rows, but it is memory intensive and most effective when read hotspots are stable.
